optionalActivities.title: Change one parent and keep only the reasoning that still applies
optionalActivities.originalCompleteSection:
Change one parent and keep only the reasoning that still applies

A grower now keeps the RrTt parent but replaces the rrTt parent with an rrtt plant. The allele meanings and the independent-assortment model are unchanged.

The one change to the tomato cross
CaseParent 1Parent 2
Worked crossRrTtrrTt
New crossRrTtrrtt

Which parental gamete list stays the same, and which must change? Give both lists and the new grid dimensions. Use them to find the proportion of offspring that will be short, and decide whether the earlier red/yellow proportions still hold. Explain why each retained or revised prediction follows from the allele contributions.

This practice is optional and ungraded. Save your reasoning, then open the comparison deliberately. It does not count toward required chapter progress.

Optional response. Select Save response to collect it. Maximum 5000 characters.

Optional hint: locate the changed allele pair

Only the second parent's height pair changed. Which colour allele must that parent contribute? Which height allele must it now contribute? Compare the resulting gamete with each of the first parent's four types.

Compare the retained and revised reasoning

The RrTt parent still produces RT, Rt, rT and rt, each with probability ¼. rrtt contributes r at the colour locus and t at the height locus, so its only distinct gamete is rt, with probability 1. A four-row, one-column grid is sufficient.

Complete comparison for RrTt × rrtt
RrTt gameterrtt gameteOffspring genotype and phenotype
RTrtRrTt — red, tall
RtrtRrtt — red, short
rTrtrrTt — yellow, tall
rtrtrrtt — yellow, short

Each genotype has probability ¼ × 1 = ¼, so the four genotype probabilities total 1. They also give four different phenotypes, each with probability ¼. Two cells are tt: the short proportion is 2/4 = ½, and the other half are tall. The old ¼ short prediction no longer applies because the second parent always supplies t instead of supplying T or t.

The colour cross remains Rr × rr. Half the offspring receive R from the first parent and are Rr, red; half receive r and are rr, yellow. Thus the overall red/yellow proportions remain ½ and ½ even though the four joint colour/height probabilities have changed. The unchanged colour conclusion and the changed height conclusion come from different loci.

Check your response: keep the first parent's list; reduce the second to rt; size the grid from those lists; show the two tt outcomes; explain why the overall colour proportions survive while the height probability changes. A four-by-two grid could use two identical rt columns with appropriate weights, but that would add an unnecessary duplicate, not another gamete type. Retaining the old rT column would be a different error: rrtt cannot contribute T.

optionalActivities.title: Decide what the new offspring settles—and what it leaves open
optionalActivities.originalCompleteSection:
Decide what the new offspring settles—and what it leaves open

Use this hypothetical plant model. V is completely dominant for violet flowers; vv gives white flowers. L is completely dominant for smooth leaves; ll gives lobed leaves. The loci assort independently, the stated parentage is known, and these genotype-to-phenotype rules apply reliably.

A breeding record with incomplete parental genotypes
RecordFlower and leaf phenotypeWhat is already known about the genotype
Parent 1Violet flowers, lobed leavesV_ll
Parent 2White flowers, smooth leavesvvL_
One observed offspringWhite flowers, smooth leavesUse the phenotype rules to determine what is forced and what remains possible.

A classmate says that this offspring must fill both parental blanks, just as the yellow, spherical squash offspring did. Evaluate that claim. Identify the allele each parent had to contribute to this offspring, state which parental genotype is now forced and which possibilities remain for the other parent, and name a further offspring leaf phenotype that would settle the remaining blank. Explain whether a finite run of smooth-leaf offspring alone would settle it.

This practice is optional and ungraded. Save your first explanation, then intentionally open the comparison. It does not count toward required chapter progress.

Optional response. Select Save response to collect it. Maximum 5000 characters.

Optional hint: inspect each missing allele separately

White flowers require vv, so trace one v back to each parent. For the leaves, the lobed parent can contribute only l. A smooth child must also have L, but does that tell you whether the other parent has a second L or an l?

Compare the evidence and its limit

The white offspring is vv, so each parent supplied v. Parent 1 already showed the violet phenotype and therefore had V; supplying v forces it to be Vvll. Parent 2 was already known to be vv. For leaf shape, parent 1 supplies l. The smooth offspring must have received L from parent 2, giving the offspring vvLl. The actual gamete contributions to this offspring were vl from parent 1 and vL from parent 2.

Parent 2 could still be vvLL or vvLl. Both can supply vL, so this observed offspring does not reveal the second leaf-shape allele. The classmate's claim goes too far: in the squash example the offspring expressed the recessive form at both loci and required both recessive contributions; here smooth leaves show that L was supplied, not that parent 2 lacks l.

A further lobed-leaf offspring would be ll. Parent 1 supplies l, so the second l would have to come from parent 2, forcing that parent to be vvLl. If parent 2 is vvLL, it contributes L every time and all offspring are smooth. If it is vvLl, its L and l contributions make both smooth and lobed offspring possible. A finite run containing only smooth offspring is possible under either candidate; it does not logically force LL. You do not need to assign a probability to the two possible parents to state this limit.

Check your response: force Vvll for parent 1 using the observed v contribution; retain both vvLL and vvLl for parent 2; identify the observed child's Ll pair and the vL contribution; explain why an ll child would settle the second blank but smooth-only observations do not prove it.

mc.prompt: What assumption is needed for multiplying separate two-locus probabilities in these examples?
mc.answer: The loci assort independently under the model
mc.explanation: Independence allows the product rule for locus outcomes.
mc.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.
options: The loci assort independently under the model
The two genes must be identical
Each offspring compensates for the previous one

mc.prompt: Use the stated pea model: TT and Tt are tall, tt is short; GG and Gg give green pods, gg gives yellow pods. Two TtGg parents are crossed with ordinary segregation, independent assortment, random fertilisation and reliable phenotype expression. For one offspring, what is the probability of being short or having yellow pods, including an offspring with both characteristics? The denominator includes all possible offspring, not only those showing one of these traits.
mc.explanation: Count three non-overlapping phenotype groups: short/green has probability 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16; tall/yellow has probability 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16; short/yellow has probability 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Adding these mutually exclusive groups gives 7/16. The double-recessive offspring qualifies, but counts once. The remaining tall/green group is 9/16, so all four groups total 1. Choosing 1/16 counts only the offspring with both recessive phenotypes; 3/16 counts only one single-recessive group. Adding 1/4 short to 1/4 yellow to get 1/2 would count short/yellow offspring twice.
mc.cue: Separate the qualifying offspring into short/green, tall/yellow and short/yellow. Count each possible offspring in only one of those groups.

writing.prompt: A/a and B/b are alleles at two independently assorting autosomal loci. For AaBB × AaBb, a student intends each table header to name one distinct possible gamete type. The two row headers for AaBB are AB and aB. The four column headers for AaBb are AB, Ab, ab and ab. The student says, ‘A two-by-four table has eight boxes, so every possible gamete pairing is included once.’ Evaluate and repair the table. Derive the complete gamete list and probabilities for each parent, identify the defect in the proposed headers, and justify the probability of each cell in the corrected table. Assume ordinary equal segregation and random fertilisation.
writing.model: AaBB supplies A or a at the first locus, each with probability 1/2, and B at the second with probability 1. Its distinct gametes are AB and aB, each 1/2; the proposed rows are correct. AaBb supplies A or a and B or b, each at one half. Independent assortment gives AB, Ab, aB and ab, each 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The proposed columns omit aB and repeat ab. Replace one ab header with aB. The dimensions can remain two by four, but the lists now include every distinct possible contribution. Eight boxes alone did not establish that: the original arrangement omitted valid pairings involving the second parent's aB gamete. Merely adjusting the weights of the repeated ab columns would not restore that missing type. In the corrected table, random fertilisation gives each pairing probability 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8. Each parent's gamete probabilities total 1, and the eight cell probabilities total 8 × 1/8 = 1. A transposed four-by-two table with the same correct lists and weights is equally valid.
criteria: Derives AB and aB at 1/2 each for AaBB, using the certain B contribution.
Derives AB, Ab, aB and ab at 1/4 each for AaBb from ordinary segregation and independent assortment.
Identifies both the missing aB and the duplicated ab; repairs the list and explains why correct dimensions alone do not show completeness.
Justifies each corrected pairing as 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8 under random fertilisation and checks the gamete and cell probabilities total 1.

writing.prompt: In a hypothetical plant model, CC and Cc give coloured petals, cc gives white petals; HH and Hh give hairy stems, hh gives smooth stems. Two CcHh parents are crossed with ordinary segregation, independent assortment, random fertilisation and reliable expression. A student predicts that 9/16 of their offspring will be homozygous at each of the two loci because 9/16 have coloured petals and hairy stems. Evaluate the prediction. List the offspring genotypes that are homozygous at both loci and calculate their combined probability for one offspring, showing the allele contributions or separate-locus probabilities and justifying your operations.
writing.model: The prediction confuses genotype with phenotype. Each CcHh parent can make CH, Ch, cH and ch gametes, each with probability 1/4 under independent assortment. At the C locus, Cc × Cc gives 1/4 CC, 1/2 Cc and 1/4 cc. Homozygosity includes CC or cc, so add these exclusive alternatives: 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. At the H locus, Hh × Hh similarly gives 1/4 HH, 1/2 Hh and 1/4 hh, with homozygosity probability 1/2. The question requires homozygosity at both independent loci, so multiply 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The qualifying genotypes are CCHH, CChh, ccHH and cchh. Each occurs in one of the sixteen equally likely gamete pairings, so their combined probability is 4/16, confirming 1/4. The other twelve pairings contain heterozygosity at one or both loci; 4/16 + 12/16 = 1. The 9/16 coloured/hairy group also includes CCHh, CcHH and CcHh, which are heterozygous at one or both loci. Conversely, some double-homozygous offspring express a recessive phenotype. Dominant appearance therefore does not identify the requested genotype group.
criteria: Distinguishes homozygosity at each locus from expression of both dominant phenotypes.
Identifies all four qualifying genotypes: CCHH, CChh, ccHH and cchh.
Derives each single-locus homozygosity probability as 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 and multiplies the two independent requirements, or gives an equivalent correctly weighted sixteen-pairing method.
Concludes 1/4, checks the counted possibilities, and explains why the 9/16 coloured/hairy group includes genotypes that do not qualify.

worked.title: Solve a two-locus cross without unnecessary boxes
worked.scenario: In an independent complete-dominance model, RrTt × rrTt produces offspring. Find the probability of red, short offspring: R_tt.
steps: At the colour locus, Rr × rr gives P(R_) = 1/2.
At the height locus, Tt × Tt gives P(tt) = 1/4.
Both conditions are required, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.
For 80 offspring the expected count is 80 × 1/8 = 10.
The result relies on independence of the two loci.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A DNA sequence that contributes to a functional product or inherited characteristic.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A DNA region influences a pigment-producing process.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A gene and a particular version of that gene are different concepts.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A DNA region influences a pigment-producing process.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A DNA region influences a pigment-producing process.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A gene and a particular version of that gene are different concepts.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: An alternative version of a gene.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Two versions at the same locus are represented as B and b.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A diploid individual usually carries two alleles at an autosomal locus, even when more exist in the population.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Two versions at the same locus are represented as B and b.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Two versions at the same locus are represented as B and b.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A diploid individual usually carries two alleles at an autosomal locus, even when more exist in the population.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: The allele combination an organism carries at the locus or loci being considered.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A model organism is Bb for a pigment gene.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Genotype records the allele combination, not just the appearance.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A model organism is Bb for a pigment gene.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A model organism is Bb for a pigment gene.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Genotype records the allele combination, not just the appearance.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: An observable or measurable characteristic resulting from genotype and its biological context.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A model organism produces dark pigment.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Phenotypes can include physiological or behavioural traits, not only colour.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A model organism produces dark pigment.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A model organism produces dark pigment.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Phenotypes can include physiological or behavioural traits, not only colour.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: The separation of the two alleles at a locus into different gametes.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A heterozygous Rr parent produces R and r gametes in the simple model.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: The parent has both alleles, but an individual gamete receives one.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A heterozygous Rr parent produces R and r gametes in the simple model.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A heterozygous Rr parent produces R and r gametes in the simple model.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: The parent has both alleles, but an individual gamete receives one.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Producing offspring with the same trait when bred within the line under the stated conditions.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A homozygous pea line repeatedly produces the same flower phenotype.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: In Mendel’s simple models, true-breeding lines are homozygous for the studied trait.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A homozygous pea line repeatedly produces the same flower phenotype.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A homozygous pea line repeatedly produces the same flower phenotype.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: In Mendel’s simple models, true-breeding lines are homozygous for the studied trait.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: The first offspring generation from a specified parental cross.
all56ExistingTerms.example: RR crossed with rr produces a first generation of Rr offspring.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: F1 names a relationship to a cross, not a universal genotype.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: RR crossed with rr produces a first generation of Rr offspring.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: RR crossed with rr produces a first generation of Rr offspring.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: F1 names a relationship to a cross, not a universal genotype.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: The generation produced from the F1 in the specified breeding design.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Two F1 heterozygotes are crossed to examine the next generation.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Its ratios depend on the parental genotypes and assumptions.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Two F1 heterozygotes are crossed to examine the next generation.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Two F1 heterozygotes are crossed to examine the next generation.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Its ratios depend on the parental genotypes and assumptions.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A table combining possible parental gametes to organize offspring genotypes.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Rows list one parent’s gametes and columns the other’s.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Each cell represents a possible combination, not a separate guaranteed offspring.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Rows list one parent’s gametes and columns the other’s.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Rows list one parent’s gametes and columns the other’s.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Each cell represents a possible combination, not a separate guaranteed offspring.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A cross between individuals heterozygous for one studied gene.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Aa × Aa is used to examine segregation of one locus.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A single-trait cross is not always heterozygote × heterozygote.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Aa × Aa is used to examine segregation of one locus.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Aa × Aa is used to examine segregation of one locus.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A single-trait cross is not always heterozygote × heterozygote.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: The expected proportion of an outcome under specified conditions.
all56ExistingTerms.example: One of four equally likely combinations is homozygous recessive.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Use the group asked about as the denominator.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: One of four equally likely combinations is homozygous recessive.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: One of four equally likely combinations is homozygous recessive.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Use the group asked about as the denominator.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: The predicted count obtained by multiplying a probability by the sample size.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A probability of 0.25 in 80 offspring gives an expected count of 20.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: An expected count need not equal an observed count.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A probability of 0.25 in 80 offspring gives an expected count of 20.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A probability of 0.25 in 80 offspring gives an expected count of 20.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: An expected count need not equal an observed count.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A cross with a homozygous recessive individual used to investigate an unknown genotype.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A dark B_ individual is crossed with a pale bb tester.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: One recessive offspring can be informative; all dominant offspring in a small sample need not prove homozygosity.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A dark B_ individual is crossed with a pale bb tester.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A dark B_ individual is crossed with a pale bb tester.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: One recessive offspring can be informative; all dominant offspring in a small sample need not prove homozygosity.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Having two identical alleles at a locus.
all56ExistingTerms.example: An individual is AA or aa rather than Aa.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Homozygous can be dominant or recessive.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: An individual is AA or aa rather than Aa.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: An individual is AA or aa rather than Aa.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Homozygous can be dominant or recessive.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Having two different alleles at a locus.
all56ExistingTerms.example: An individual has one dominant and one recessive allele in a simple model.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A heterozygote can share a phenotype with a homozygous dominant individual.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: An individual has one dominant and one recessive allele in a simple model.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: An individual has one dominant and one recessive allele in a simple model.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A heterozygote can share a phenotype with a homozygous dominant individual.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Differences between observed sample outcomes and their expected proportions due to chance.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A small set of offspring contains no recessive individual even though each had a one-half chance.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A small sample may not distinguish two models decisively.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A small set of offspring contains no recessive individual even though each had a one-half chance.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A small set of offspring contains no recessive individual even though each had a one-half chance.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A small sample may not distinguish two models decisively.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A cross between individuals heterozygous at two studied loci.
all56ExistingTerms.example: AaBb × AaBb is used to examine two traits under stated assumptions.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: The familiar 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio needs complete dominance and independent assortment.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: AaBb × AaBb is used to examine two traits under stated assumptions.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: AaBb × AaBb is used to examine two traits under stated assumptions.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: The familiar 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio needs complete dominance and independent assortment.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Independent segregation of alleles at different loci when the chromosome arrangement permits it.
all56ExistingTerms.example: An AaBb individual produces AB, Ab, aB and ab equally in an unlinked model.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Linked genes can depart from this equal-combination prediction.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: An AaBb individual produces AB, Ab, aB and ab equally in an unlinked model.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: An AaBb individual produces AB, Ab, aB and ab equally in an unlinked model.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Linked genes can depart from this equal-combination prediction.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Multiplication of probabilities for specified independent events.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Probability of aa and bb is calculated as P(aa) × P(bb) when the loci assort independently.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Check independence before multiplying separate trait probabilities.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Probability of aa and bb is calculated as P(aa) × P(bb) when the loci assort independently.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Probability of aa and bb is calculated as P(aa) × P(bb) when the loci assort independently.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Check independence before multiplying separate trait probabilities.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: The set of one allele from each studied locus carried by a gamete.
all56ExistingTerms.example: An AaBb parent can produce an Ab gamete in an independent model.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A gamete does not receive both A and a at the same autosomal locus in this model.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: An AaBb parent can produce an Ab gamete in an independent model.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: An AaBb parent can produce an Ab gamete in an independent model.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A gamete does not receive both A and a at the same autosomal locus in this model.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: An allele relationship in which the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Red and white flower alleles produce pink flowers in the specified heterozygote model.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: An intermediate phenotype does not mean the alleles permanently blend.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Red and white flower alleles produce pink flowers in the specified heterozygote model.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Red and white flower alleles produce pink flowers in the specified heterozygote model.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: An intermediate phenotype does not mean the alleles permanently blend.

all56ExistingTerms.feature: A roan coat contains both red and white hairs in the model.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Codominance is not limited to separate patches of cells; both products can be present in the same cells.

all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: R1R2 may be pink in one model but red-and-white in another.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: R1R2 may be pink in one model but red-and-white in another.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: The same notation does not establish the inheritance relationship without its definition.

all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: An incomplete-dominance heterozygote cross gives three distinguishable phenotype categories.

all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: The simplified ABO model includes IA, IB and i.

all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: An XY individual has only one allele at many X-linked loci.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: An allele is represented as Xb rather than as an autosomal b alone.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: An allele is represented as Xb rather than as an autosomal b alone.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: An XY individual has only one allele at many X-linked loci.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Having only one copy of a gene in the relevant chromosome context.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A typical XY individual has one copy of many X-linked genes.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Hemizygous is not the same as homozygous.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A typical XY individual has one copy of many X-linked genes.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A typical XY individual has one copy of many X-linked genes.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Hemizygous is not the same as homozygous.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Probability calculated within a stated subgroup or condition.
all56ExistingTerms.example: The question asks what fraction of sons are affected, not what fraction of all children are affected sons.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Changing the denominator can change the numerical answer.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: The question asks what fraction of sons are affected, not what fraction of all children are affected sons.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: The question asks what fraction of sons are affected, not what fraction of all children are affected sons.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Changing the denominator can change the numerical answer.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: An inheritance model in which the recessive allele is on X and is expressed in a hemizygous XY individual.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A carrier XX parent can have an affected XY offspring.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: An affected father does not transmit his X to sons in the typical XX/XY model.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A carrier XX parent can have an affected XY offspring.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A carrier XX parent can have an affected XY offspring.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: An affected father does not transmit his X to sons in the typical XX/XY model.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Inheritance in which multiple genes contribute to a trait.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Several gene regions contribute to variation in height.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Polygenic does not mean many alleles at only one locus.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Several gene regions contribute to variation in height.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Several gene regions contribute to variation in height.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Polygenic does not mean many alleles at only one locus.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A range of phenotype values without only a few sharply separated categories.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A class has a range of measured heights rather than only tall and short genotypes.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Continuous measurements can reflect both genetic and environmental contributions.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A class has a range of measured heights rather than only tall and short genotypes.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A class has a range of measured heights rather than only tall and short genotypes.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Continuous measurements can reflect both genetic and environmental contributions.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: An effect of conditions such as nutrition or temperature on phenotype.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Plants with similar genotypes grow to different sizes under different resource conditions.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: An environmental effect does not necessarily change the inherited DNA sequence.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Plants with similar genotypes grow to different sizes under different resource conditions.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Plants with similar genotypes grow to different sizes under different resource conditions.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: An environmental effect does not necessarily change the inherited DNA sequence.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Use of genetic information to produce functional products in cells.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Cells make different proteins under different developmental or environmental conditions.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Expression can change without changing the allele sequence.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Cells make different proteins under different developmental or environmental conditions.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Cells make different proteins under different developmental or environmental conditions.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Expression can change without changing the allele sequence.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A diagram tracing a specified trait through family relationships across generations.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Symbols connected by parent–offspring lines show which relatives express a trait.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A pedigree is evidence to test a model, not proof that one clue is always decisive.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Symbols connected by parent–offspring lines show which relatives express a trait.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Symbols connected by parent–offspring lines show which relatives express a trait.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A pedigree is evidence to test a model, not proof that one clue is always decisive.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A model in which a trait is expressed when two recessive alleles occur at an autosomal locus.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Two unaffected Aa parents can have an affected aa child.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Unaffected individuals can be AA or Aa.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Two unaffected Aa parents can have an affected aa child.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Two unaffected Aa parents can have an affected aa child.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Unaffected individuals can be AA or Aa.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A model in which one dominant allele at an autosomal locus is sufficient for expression under the stated assumptions.
all56ExistingTerms.example: An affected Dd individual and unaffected dd partner can have affected or unaffected children.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Affected individuals can be DD or Dd unless other evidence resolves the genotype.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: An affected Dd individual and unaffected dd partner can have affected or unaffected children.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: An affected Dd individual and unaffected dd partner can have affected or unaffected children.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Affected individuals can be DD or Dd unless other evidence resolves the genotype.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A level of descent in a family diagram, commonly labelled with a Roman numeral.
all56ExistingTerms.example: I, II and III distinguish successive levels in a pedigree.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Individual numbers identify people within a generation.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: I, II and III distinguish successive levels in a pedigree.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: I, II and III distinguish successive levels in a pedigree.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Individual numbers identify people within a generation.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A simple model in which a dominant allele on X produces the trait under specified penetrance assumptions.
all56ExistingTerms.example: An affected father transmits his affected X to all daughters in the typical model.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: No direct paternal X is transmitted to a son.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: An affected father transmits his affected X to all daughters in the typical model.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: An affected father transmits his affected X to all daughters in the typical model.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: No direct paternal X is transmitted to a son.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: The proportion of individuals with a genotype who express the associated phenotype.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A simple pedigree question assumes every person with a specified genotype expresses the trait.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Incomplete penetrance can make patterns less straightforward than classroom models.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A simple pedigree question assumes every person with a specified genotype expresses the trait.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A simple pedigree question assumes every person with a specified genotype expresses the trait.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Incomplete penetrance can make patterns less straightforward than classroom models.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A possible inheritance explanation tested against the observed relationships and traits.
all56ExistingTerms.example: An X-linked recessive hypothesis is checked for contradictions in every branch.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A model consistent with a small family need not be the only possible explanation.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: An X-linked recessive hypothesis is checked for contradictions in every branch.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: An X-linked recessive hypothesis is checked for contradictions in every branch.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A model consistent with a small family need not be the only possible explanation.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: An individual who must carry a recessive allele under the stated pedigree model.
all56ExistingTerms.example: An unaffected mother of an affected son carries the relevant X-linked recessive allele when other assumptions hold.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: The conclusion depends on the model and relationship information.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: An unaffected mother of an affected son carries the relevant X-linked recessive allele when other assumptions hold.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: An unaffected mother of an affected son carries the relevant X-linked recessive allele when other assumptions hold.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: The conclusion depends on the model and relationship information.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Genes on the same chromosome that may be inherited together, especially when close.
all56ExistingTerms.example: AB is carried on one homologue and ab on the other.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Physical linkage can reduce recombinant frequency, but widely separated loci may appear independent.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: AB is carried on one homologue and ab on the other.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: AB is carried on one homologue and ab on the other.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Physical linkage can reduce recombinant frequency, but widely separated loci may appear independent.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: An allele combination matching one of the original chromosome arrangements in the heterozygous parent.
all56ExistingTerms.example: For AB/ab, the combinations AB and ab are parental.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Parental depends on the specified phase, not always capital letters together.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: For AB/ab, the combinations AB and ab are parental.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: For AB/ab, the combinations AB and ab are parental.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Parental depends on the specified phase, not always capital letters together.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: An allele combination different from the parent’s original arrangement for the loci considered.
all56ExistingTerms.example: For AB/ab, crossing over can generate Ab and aB.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Recombinant does not necessarily mean a new allele was created.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: For AB/ab, crossing over can generate Ab and aB.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: For AB/ab, crossing over can generate Ab and aB.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Recombinant does not necessarily mean a new allele was created.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: The arrangement of alleles across the two homologous chromosomes.
all56ExistingTerms.example: AB/ab differs from Ab/aB even though both can be written AaBb.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: The compact genotype AaBb alone does not specify phase.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: AB/ab differs from Ab/aB even though both can be written AaBb.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: AB/ab differs from Ab/aB even though both can be written AaBb.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: The compact genotype AaBb alone does not specify phase.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: The fraction of scored offspring or gametes that are recombinant for the loci considered.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Eighteen of 100 test-cross offspring are recombinant, giving 18%.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Use all scored offspring in the denominator and both recombinant classes in the numerator.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Eighteen of 100 test-cross offspring are recombinant, giving 18%.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Eighteen of 100 test-cross offspring are recombinant, giving 18%.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Use all scored offspring in the denominator and both recombinant classes in the numerator.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A unit of genetic map distance corresponding approximately to one percent recombination over short intervals.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A short interval with about 8% recombinants is estimated as about 8 map units.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A map unit is not a universal fixed number of base pairs.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A short interval with about 8% recombinants is estimated as about 8 map units.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A short interval with about 8% recombinants is estimated as about 8 map units.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A map unit is not a universal fixed number of base pairs.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A map of relative gene order and distances estimated from recombination data.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Genes A, B and C are placed along a line with measured intervals.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A genetic map is not a direct microscopic measurement of DNA length.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Genes A, B and C are placed along a line with measured intervals.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Genes A, B and C are placed along a line with measured intervals.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A genetic map is not a direct microscopic measurement of DNA length.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Two exchange events within a chromosome region.
all56ExistingTerms.example: Two exchanges can restore the original outside-marker arrangement.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Undetected multiple crossovers can make observed two-locus recombination underestimate longer distances.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: Two exchanges can restore the original outside-marker arrangement.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: Two exchanges can restore the original outside-marker arrangement.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Undetected multiple crossovers can make observed two-locus recombination underestimate longer distances.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Analysis of genetic material or related markers to investigate particular variants or conditions.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A test checks for a specified DNA variant.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: A test’s scope determines what a negative or positive result can establish.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A test checks for a specified DNA variant.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A test checks for a specified DNA variant.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: A test’s scope determines what a negative or positive result can establish.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A process helping people understand genetic information, inheritance and possible implications for their choices.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A professional explains a result, its uncertainty and relevant family context.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Counselling supports informed decisions rather than dictating one choice for every family.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A professional explains a result, its uncertainty and relevant family context.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A professional explains a result, its uncertainty and relevant family context.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Counselling supports informed decisions rather than dictating one choice for every family.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: Agreement based on understanding the purpose, potential benefits, risks and alternatives of a procedure or study.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A participant considers how a genetic sample and results will be used before agreeing.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Consent involves more than the physical act of giving a sample.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A participant considers how a genetic sample and results will be used before agreeing.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A participant considers how a genetic sample and results will be used before agreeing.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Consent involves more than the physical act of giving a sample.

all56ExistingTerms.meaning: A probability or increased likelihood associated with genetic information in a specified context.
all56ExistingTerms.example: A variant is associated with increased probability of a condition without making it inevitable.
all56ExistingTerms.importantDistinction: Risk is not the same as certainty.
all56ExistingTerms.whatItDoes: A variant is associated with increased probability of a condition without making it inevitable.
all56ExistingTerms.feature: A variant is associated with increased probability of a condition without making it inevitable.
all56ExistingTerms.confusion: Risk is not the same as certainty.
